strengths: Novel and well-motivated idea: repurposing a pretrained multi-view diffusion model (SV3D-p) as a geometric feature extractor and unprojecting its intermediate decoder features into explicit 3D feature volumes for keypoint discovery. This is a creative way to transform implicit diffusion priors into explicit 3D structure.

Addresses a genuinely hard and underexplored problem: unsupervised monocular 3D keypoint estimation, which avoids the need for manual 3D annotations and calibrated multi-view captures that dominate prior work.

Competitive quantitative results on Human3.6M: the method outperforms unsupervised single-view baselines (KeypointNet, Honari et al.) and even reaches competitive P-MPJE with multi-view methods, despite using only a single image at inference.

Meaningful generalization demonstrations: despite training only on human data, the model produces plausible keypoints on in-the-wild (DAVIS) and out-of-domain (GSO, AP-10K, Stanford Dogs) categories, which supports the generality claim.

Ablation studies (Table 2) provide useful evidence: replacing diffusion features with ResNet features degrades performance, and increasing virtual viewpoints beyond K=3 yields diminishing returns, supporting the design choices.
Additional downstream application (animatable 3D object generation via MST edges and Gaussian skinning weights) adds practical value beyond keypoint estimation.
Clarity of the method exposition: the pipeline (feature aggregation, 2D-to-3D lifting, self-supervised training) is described coherently with clear equations.
weaknesses: The 'unsupervised' framing is somewhat overstated: the method depends heavily on a large-scale pretrained multi-view diffusion model (SV3D-p) and on Grounded SAM for foreground masking. These models encode substantial learned priors, so the method is better described as 'annotation-free' rather than fully unsupervised. The dependence on the quality of these pretrained components is acknowledged but not deeply analyzed.

Quantitative evaluation breadth is limited: Human3.6M is the only dataset with a full quantitative benchmark. Generalization to animals and out-of-domain objects is presented almost entirely qualitatively (Figs. 4, 5), making the generalization claims hard to verify rigorously.
Some experimental details and ablations are deferred to the supplement (additional ablations, more object categories), which makes the main paper's evidence for certain claims incomplete.

Fairness of comparison is not fully established: the method leverages a strong pretrained diffusion backbone while some baselines (e.g., KeypointNet, Honari et al.) are trained without such priors; the comparison does not control for the extra pretrained capacity, and the effect of the diffusion backbone's own training data is not discussed.
No quantitative comparison on animal datasets (e.g., AP-10K, Stanford Dogs) despite these being used for generalization claims; only visual results are shown.

Computational cost is acknowledged as a limitation (multiple denoising steps for feature extraction), but no runtime/throughput numbers are provided to quantify this, which matters for practical adoption.

The edge/keypoint connectivity and skinning pipeline is described only briefly; details (e.g., how MST is combined with predicted edge weights) are insufficient to fully reproduce the animatable-object results.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated formulation: the paper repurposes a pretrained multi-view diffusion model (SV3D-p) both as a generator of multi-view supervision and as a multi-view feature extractor, unprojecting its intermediate decoder features into an explicit 3D feature volume. Turning implicit diffusion priors into explicit geometric features for monocular 3D keypoint discovery is a fresh and non-trivial idea.

Competitive quantitative results on Human3.6M in the single-view inference setting: with a 2-hidden-layer MLP regressor the method reaches 121.34 MPJPE / 118.29 N-MPJPE / 85.26 P-MPJPE, surpassing unsupervised single-view baselines (KeypointNet 112.9, Honari single-view 89.05 P-MPJPE, Sosa 96.4) and approaching multi-view methods such as BKinD-3D, despite using only a single image at inference.

Impressive qualitative generalization: consistent keypoints on DAVIS in-the-wild humans, GSO out-of-domain objects, unseen dog breeds (Stanford Dogs), and unseen species (giraffe, rhino, horse, tiger) without any animal- or object-specific supervision, demonstrating robustness of the diffusion-prior approach.

Practical downstream utility: a complete pipeline that converts predicted 3D keypoints and edge graphs into an animatable 3D object (MST skeleton plus Gaussian-based skinning weights), enabling manipulation of diffusion-generated 3D assets without manual rigging.

Ablations are informative and support the design: replacing diffusion features with ResNet features on the same generated views degrades performance substantially (138.97 vs. 121.34 MPJPE for the MLP regressor), isolating the value of the diffusion feature extractor; the view-count study shows saturation around K=3-4.

Reproducibility is reasonable: the backbone (SV3D-p), timestep (tau=500), grid resolution (M=72), keypoint count (N=18), optimizer, learning rates, hardware, and loss weights are all specified, and code is promised.
weaknesses: Evaluation breadth is limited quantitatively. Only Human3.6M has numeric results; the generalization claims on Stanford Dogs, AP-10K, DAVIS, and GSO are entirely qualitative, even though AP-10K and Stanford Dogs provide annotations that would permit quantitative keypoint error. The animatable-model pipeline is also evaluated only visually, with no metric for skeleton/skinning quality or manipulation fidelity.

The 'unsupervised' framing is overstated. The method depends on a pretrained multi-view diffusion model (SV3D-p, trained on large-scale 3D data) and Grounded SAM for foreground masks. This is annotation-free/zero-shot with strong pretrained priors rather than unsupervised learning, and the paper does not discuss possible data overlap between the pretrained model's training corpus and the evaluation sets (e.g., Human3.6M subjects).

Some claims are stronger than the evidence. The statement that the method 'outperforms all unsupervised single-view baselines' is only true for certain regressors: Kundu et al. [24] reports 79.3 P-MPJPE versus Ours' 85.26, and the claim of 'improved P-MPJPE compared to monocular human pose estimation methods employing human-specific priors' does not hold against that entry. The paper should qualify these comparisons (regressor type, subset protocol, human-specific priors) more carefully.

The model is trained per dataset (Human3.6M for humans, then Stanford Dogs for dogs), so it is not a single category-agnostic model. This undercuts the 'diverse object categories' claim, since the reported generalization benefits partly from category-specific training on the same distribution.

A key assumption—that the diffusion backbone learns a sufficiently consistent 3D/world coordinate system for unprojection into a shared canonical volume—is central to the method but is not analyzed or validated. There is no diagnostic of cross-view geometric consistency, and no error bars or statistical reporting on the Human3.6M numbers.

Inference cost is acknowledged only qualitatively. Running multiple denoising steps and caching intermediate features is significantly more expensive than feed-forward alternatives, but no runtime or memory measurements are provided, and the ablation does not compare the cost/accuracy trade-off against baselines.

strengths: Proposes a novel and timely framework, KeyDiff3D, that repurposes a pretrained multi-view diffusion model (SV3D-p) as a geometry-aware feature extractor and uses generated multi-view images as supervision for unsupervised monocular 3D keypoint discovery. The combination of diffusion features, 3D volumetric lifting, and reconstruction-based self-supervision is reasonably designed.

Provides a complete pipeline from single-image input to 3D keypoints, edge graphs, and an animatable 3D object manipulation application, demonstrating the potential of diffusion priors for 3D structural understanding.

Reports quantitative results on Human3.6M showing improvements over several unsupervised single-view baselines (e.g., Keypoint-net [47] and Honari et al. [11] single-view) under MPJPE, N-MPJPE, and P-MPJPE, and includes an ablation indicating that diffusion features outperform ResNet features applied to generated views.
Shows qualitative generalization to in-the-wild and out-of-domain examples (DAVIS, GSO, AP-10K, Stanford Dogs), suggesting the method can discover plausible keypoints beyond the training domain.
Implementation details such as datasets, optimization settings, diffusion timestep, number of views, voxel resolution, and code availability are partially provided, supporting some reproducibility.
weaknesses: The empirical evidence is insufficient for the central claims. Only Human3.6M is quantitatively evaluated. Claims of generalization to Stanford Dogs, DAVIS, GSO, and AP-10K are supported solely by qualitative figures, with no PCK/APK or other error metrics on unseen species or out-of-domain images. This is a major gap for a paper whose main contribution is generalization.

The claim that the method is 'competitive with multi-view baselines' is overstated. Table 1 shows Honari et al. [11] with 4 views and 2-hidden-layer MLP achieves 73.8 MPJPE, and Yang et al. [58] achieves 85.6 MPJPE, while the proposed method's best full-set result is 119.07/121.34 MPJPE. The method only surpasses BKinD-3D. Additionally, 'Ours*' results on a six-action simplified subset (85.47 MPJPE) are not compared against baselines on the same subset, making them potentially misleading.

The main paper lacks ablations for core design choices. There is no ablation on the edge map, adjacency matrix, mask loss, feature aggregation, diffusion timestep tau, voxel resolution M, number of keypoints N, or reconstruction network design. Only two factors (diffusion features vs. ResNet and number of views) are ablated in the main text. Many central claims about why the method works remain unvalidated.

Several technical details necessary to assess correctness and reproducibility are missing or vague: how camera parameters for the input view are obtained and how canonical coordinate alignment is achieved; the architecture of the feature aggregation network, keypoint head, 3D convolutional network, and reconstruction network; how the differentiable Gaussian line maps and edge maps are rendered; how the MST edge weights and skinning weights are computed; and how the manipulation poses in Fig. 6 are generated. The method cannot be fully reproduced from the main paper.

The 'unsupervised' characterization is qualified: the method depends on a large pretrained multi-view diffusion model (SV3D-p) and Grounded SAM, both trained with external supervision and large-scale data. The paper does not analyze what geometric priors are inherited, how sensitive the method is to these models, or how it avoids their biases. The term 'unsupervised' should be more carefully scoped.

The keypoint semantics are not analyzed. The method uses a fixed number of keypoints (e.g., 18 or 32) with no explicit joint definition, and the mask loss may encourage keypoints to cover foreground regions rather than correspond to semantic joints. There is no analysis of the learned adjacency matrix or edge graphs, and no guarantee that the discovered keypoints are meaningful across categories.

The animatable 3D object manipulation pipeline is preliminary. It is evaluated only qualitatively on a few examples (Fig. 6), with no quantitative comparison, no user study, and no failure analysis. Its connection to the core keypoint estimation is not rigorously established, and it adds limited validated contribution.

The evaluation protocol has additional issues: no error bars or statistical significance; no discussion of failure cases; the comparison to some baselines may be confounded by different training data/supervision (e.g., generated multi-view vs. real multi-view); and the paper relies heavily on supplements for additional results, leaving the main paper not self-contained for assessment.

The paper acknowledges computational cost but provides no efficiency analysis. Inference requires multiple denoising steps of a diffusion model, which may be impractical. The limitations section does not discuss the lack of quantitative animal/manipulation evaluation or the missing ablations.

strengths: The core idea of exploiting intermediate multi-view diffusion features (rather than the rendered generated views themselves) as a geometric prior for 3D keypoint discovery is novel and well-motivated; the ablation in Table 3(a) showing diffusion features outperform ResNet50/CLIP/DINOv2 backbones supports this design choice.

The method addresses a genuinely challenging and relatively underexplored setting: unsupervised monocular 3D keypoint estimation without 3D annotations, camera parameters, or controlled multi-view capture, which is of practical value for scaling to arbitrary object categories.

Quantitative results on Human3.6M are competitive: with a single input view, the method (121.34 MPJPE / 118.29 N-MPJPE / 85.26 P-MPJPE) surpasses multi-view BKinD-3D trained with 2 views, and qualitative comparisons in Fig. 3 show finer-grained joints (e.g., knees) than BKinD-3D.

The paper includes a reasonably thorough set of ablations (Table 3 and Table 5): backbone choice, 3D lifting vs. 2D triangulation, number of virtual views, number of keypoints, diffusion timestep, training set size, affine transformation, view misalignment, and view aggregation.

The paper provides an honest reproduction effort (Table 4, Section A) re-training 2D baselines under identical preprocessing/splits, which strengthens the fairness of the CUB comparisons, and it transparently reports failure cases (Fig. 8: left-right ambiguity, diffusion-model dependency).

The additional pipeline for animatable 3D object generation via Gaussian Frosting and Gaussian-based skinning weights (Sec. 3.4, Fig. 6) demonstrates a useful downstream application beyond raw keypoint estimation.
weaknesses: The framing as 'unsupervised' is somewhat overstated: the method's accuracy depends critically on a large pretrained multi-view diffusion model (SV3D) whose geometric priors encode substantial 3D/multi-view supervision. This is not the same as learning geometry without any external 3D knowledge, and the paper does not clearly delimit the contribution relative to the inherited prior.

Quantitative evaluation is narrow: 3D accuracy is only measured on Human3.6M; for the animal datasets (CUB-200-2011, Stanford Dogs) and the animatable-object pipeline, only qualitative results are shown, so the generality claim is under-supported by numbers. The CUB/Stanford-Dogs comparisons are performed on projected 2D keypoints, which only indirectly reflect 3D quality.

Inference cost is substantial: Table 6 shows the full KeyDiff3D system incurs ~29.48 GB VRAM and ~11.9 s/iter, dominated by the diffusion backbone. The paper argues the added module itself is cheap, but the practical utility of the method is heavily gated by this diffusion overhead, and no accuracy-vs-cost trade-off or distillation/acceleration is explored.

Several evaluation choices deserve more scrutiny. The 3D metric relies on fitting a linear/MLP regressor from predicted keypoints to GT, which is an indirect protocol and can be sensitive to the regressor; results at N=18 (default) are not clearly aligned with standard Human3.6M joint counts, and the significance of improvements over the closest baselines (e.g., Honari et al.) is not statistically established.

Methodological dependencies on external components (Grounded-SAM/SAM for foreground masks, the diffusion model's inherent camera/coordinate system for unprojection) are non-trivial and could confound generalization claims; the reliance on the diffusion model's canonical space for 'aligned' 3D coordinates is not fully analyzed.
The animatable-model pipeline lacks any quantitative evaluation (no re-rendering metrics, no user study, no comparison to rigging baselines), so its claimed controllability is only anecdotal.

Originality is partially incremental relative to prior work (StableKeypoints, Diffusion Hyperfeatures): the main new element is extending diffusion-feature keypoint discovery to the 3D/multi-view setting, which is a sensible but not fundamentally new paradigm.

strengths: Addresses an underexplored and challenging problem: unsupervised monocular 3D keypoint discovery for arbitrary objects, without manual 3D annotations or multi-view images during training.

Proposes a technically sound pipeline that leverages multi-view diffusion model features as geometric priors, including diffusion feature aggregation, 2D-to-3D lifting, volumetric keypoint estimation, and self-supervised multi-view reconstruction.

Extensive experiments and ablations on Human3.6M, CUB-200-2011, Stanford Dogs, DAVIS, GSO, and AP-10K validate the approach and show competitive or superior performance over unsupervised single-image baselines, including BKinD-3D with two views.

Ablation studies are thorough: feature backbone, 2D vs. 3D lifting, number of virtual viewpoints, number of keypoints, diffusion timestep, training data size, affine transform, view misalignment, and view aggregation.
Demonstrates practical downstream utility by producing animatable 3D objects with predicted skeletons and skinning weights from a single image.
Clearly discusses failure cases, limitations, and computational cost, with supplementary implementation details and video results.
weaknesses: The 'unsupervised' setting is partially qualified by reliance on large pretrained models (SV3D, Grounded-SAM/SAM2) and, for Human3.6M preprocessing, on ground-truth 2D keypoint locations as SAM query points, which are manual annotations; this should be clarified and ideally replaced by a class-agnostic mask prompt.

The method still requires known camera parameters for the diffusion-generated views and unprojection, so the claim of operating 'without camera parameters' is somewhat overstated and needs precise definition.

Quantitative 3D keypoint evaluation is limited to Human3.6M; animal keypoints on CUB and Stanford Dogs are evaluated only via 2D projection or qualitatively, so 3D quality and generalization to animal categories are not fully quantified.

The animatable 3D object generation results are qualitative only, with no metrics, user study, or comparisons to rigging/animation baselines, making this contribution more demonstrative than rigorously validated.

On Human3.6M, the best reported MPJPE (119.07) remains substantially worse than multi-view methods such as Honari et al. (73.8), so the single-image advantage comes with an accuracy trade-off that should be better contextualized in the abstract and claims.

Performance depends heavily on the diffusion model's view consistency; failure cases include left-right ambiguity and diffusion generation failures, and there is no mechanism to explicitly correct these errors beyond reliance on the prior.

Reproducibility could be strengthened: no code release is mentioned, results appear single-run, and the regressor training/evaluation protocol (which uses ground-truth 3D annotations to map unsupervised keypoints) is not fully detailed in the main paper.

strengths: Introduces KeyDiff3D, a novel framework that leverages intermediate features of a pretrained multi-view diffusion model as a geometry-aware feature extractor, unprojects them into a 3D volume, and estimates 3D keypoints via a differentiable soft-argmax, avoiding 3D annotations during training.

Provides a fairly comprehensive empirical study, including ablations on diffusion backbones, 3D lifting strategies, number of virtual viewpoints, diffusion timesteps, training data size, affine transformation, and view aggregation, which supports several design choices.

Demonstrates qualitatively appealing results on diverse categories (humans, birds, dogs, out-of-domain animals) and shows a pipeline for animatable 3D object generation and manipulation from a single image.
weaknesses: The unsupervised/no-manual-annotation claim is undermined by Human3.6M preprocessing. Appendix D.3 states that SAM is prompted with '2D keypoint locations provided in the dataset' and that a bounding box is computed from 'projected 2D keypoints' for cropping. This uses ground-truth 2D annotations and leaks supervision into the main quantitative benchmark, making comparisons with unsupervised baselines unfair.

Quantitative evidence for 3D keypoint accuracy on non-human categories is limited. CUB-200-2011 and Stanford Dogs are evaluated only via projected 2D metrics or qualitatively, with no 3D ground truth. Generalization results on DAVIS, GSO, and AP-10K are qualitative only. Thus the claim of accurate 3D discovery across arbitrary categories is not fully substantiated.

Baseline comparisons on CUB are fragile. The paper relies on reproduced numbers that differ substantially from original reports (e.g., StableKeypoints CUB-align reproduced 6.38 vs. original 5.06), and on CUB-all with KP=4 Ours (7.7) is worse than StableKeypoints (5.4/5.6). The claim of matching or outperforming 2D baselines is therefore not robust.

The method is highly dependent on the quality of the pretrained multi-view diffusion model. Failure cases such as left-right ambiguity, inconsistent generated views, and missing occluded regions are shown but not quantitatively analyzed. Performance degrades when the diffusion model fails, which is a practical limitation.

The animatable 3D generation and manipulation results are qualitative only. There is no quantitative evaluation or comparison to existing rigging/animation methods, so the usefulness of this pipeline is not rigorously established.

The 'no camera parameters' claim is somewhat misleading because the pipeline still relies on known camera projection matrices for the diffusion-generated views and on foreground segmentation. The additional computational cost of the diffusion model is substantial (Table 6), which limits scalability.
